classification.difficultyReason: Recognise how differently arranged circle parts share the same area ratio, and justify equality through subdivision or equivalent area calculations.

content.prompt: Can you give a simple argument as to why the red regions in each of the unit squares below all have the same area?

spec.description: One inscribed red circle tangent to all four sides of a unit square.
spec.answerVisibility: No calculated dimensions or areas supplied.

spec.description: Red quarter circle centred at the bottom-left corner, with its arc joining top-left to bottom-right.
spec.answerVisibility: No calculated dimensions or areas supplied.

spec.description: Two inward-facing red semicircles have diameters along the left and right sides and meet at the square's centre.
spec.mathematics: Two semicircles of radius 1/2, with disjoint interiors.
spec.answerVisibility: No calculated dimensions or areas supplied.

spec.description: Four equal red circles in a two-by-two arrangement, tangent to adjacent circles and the appropriate square sides.
spec.mathematics: Four circles of radius 1/4, with disjoint interiors.
spec.answerVisibility: No calculated dimensions or areas supplied.

answer.short:
Each red region occupies $\frac{\pi}{4}$ of its unit square.

Each arrangement can be divided into smaller squares containing a scaled quarter circle.
answer.worked:
Divide the first square into four equal squares, the third into four equal squares, and the fourth into sixteen equal squares. Each small square contains a quarter circle whose radius equals that square's side. The second figure already has this form. Scaling both the quarter circle and its square preserves their area ratio:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{A_{\text{quarter circle}}}{A_{\text{square}}}&=\frac{\frac14\pi s^2}{s^2}\\\frac{A_{\text{quarter circle}}}{A_{\text{square}}}&=\frac{\pi}{4}.\end{align*}$$
Thus the red region occupies the same fraction of every unit square, so all four red areas are $\frac{\pi}{4}$ square units.
